title: CBMP-Terrestrial North American Scoping Workshop Ottawa, Canada 14-16 January 2025
text:
This workshop report is intended to summarize the Circumpolar Biodiversity Monitoring Program’s North American Terrestrial Scoping Workshop, which was conducted in Ottawa, Canada, January 14-16, 2025. The workshop was the second of 3 planned workshops which jointly will lead to the development of a new CBMP Terrestrial Implementation Plan.

1. Introduction and workshop objectives
This workshop report is intended to summarize the Circumpolar Biodiversity Monitoring Program’s
North American Terrestrial Scoping Workshop, which was conducted in Ottawa, Canada, January 14-
16, 2025. The workshop was the second of 3 planned workshops which jointly will lead to the
development of a new CBMP Terrestrial Implementation Plan.
The contents of this report capture discussions and presentations of the workshop and are not
approved by the Conservation of Arctic Flora and Fauna (CAFF) board, nor can it be construed to
represent the views of individual participants (see list of participants in Annex X).
The Terrestrial Workshop was supported by representatives from the Circumpolar Biodiversity
Monitoring Program (CBMP) Freshwater Steering Group as well as by inputs and inspirations from
the Coastal group and external invited guests as noted below.
The CBMP is an initiative of the CAFF, the biodiversity Working Group of the Arctic Council. The
CBMP aims to facilitate rapid detection, understanding, prediction, communication, and response to
significant biodiversity-related trends and pressures in the Arctic. Recognized by the UN Convention
on Biological Diversity (CBD) and as the official Arctic Biodiversity Observation Network of the Group
on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network (GEOBON), the CBMP coordinates, collects,
and synthesizes existing monitoring data from Arctic states through networks of scientists,
Indigenous organizations, and conservation groups.
The CBMP is guided by multi-year strategic plans approved by the Arctic Council, with the current
"Phase 4" covering 2021-2027. The program builds on existing monitoring networks and is
structured around four biome-specific Steering Groups: marine, coastal, freshwater, and terrestrial.
Each group has identified Focal Ecosystem Components (FECs) to monitor, prioritizing attributes
based on ecological significance, relevance to ecosystem services, value to Arctic Indigenous Peoples
and other Arctic communities, and essential management and legislation needs.
The CBMP-Terrestrial Steering Group (TSG) is currently co-led by the USA and Iceland, with
representation from all Arctic States, and the Inuit Circumpolar Council and the Saami Council have
been able to provide input into the current process. Representatives from the Inuit Circumpolar
Council participated in the workshop.
The scoping process for the TSG involves three regional workshops: one for the Nordic countries (see
report from workshop held in Copenhagen 20-22 November 2024), one in North America (this
report), and one in Russia.
Echoing the Nordic Scoping Workshop, the specific objectives of the North American Terrestrial
Scoping Workshops were to:
• Identify any new information needs of existing and potential users of CBMP monitoring data
from both within and outside the Arctic Council, including linkages to other bodies such as CBD,
GEOBON, and GBIF.
• Identify ways to better include Indigenous Knowledge in terrestrial biodiversity monitoring and
promote co-production of knowledge.
4

• Identify ways to include local knowledge and opportunities for broader citizen science
involvement.
• Improve coordination and collaboration at four levels: between CBMP-Terrestrial sub-groups,
alignment with other CBMP monitoring groups (Marine, Coastal, Freshwater), collaboration with
other Arctic Council Working Groups and ongoing CAFF projects (including Arctic Monitoring and
Assessment Programme (AMAP) and Arctic Migratory Birds Initiative (AMBI)), and collaboration
with international organizations, networks, and data holders.
• Review conceptual models in the Arctic Terrestrial Biodiversity Monitoring Plan and FECs, and
consider revisions needed based on new information. This includes identifying emerging or
changing ecosystem drivers and stressors that should be considered for monitoring and
assessment, opportunities for enhancing ecosystem-based monitoring efforts, and more holistic
and Indigenous-Knowledge led perspectives on ecosystem function and inter- relationships.
• Identify new relevant technologies and/or methodologies to be included in future monitoring,
when beneficial.
• Identify effective means for communicating CBMP outcomes, i.e., compiling and disseminating
information to decision-makers and the general public.
1.2. Background and process
Through networks of scientists, Indigenous organizations and conservation groups, CBMP
coordinates, collects and synthesizes existing biodiversity monitoring data from the Arctic. The
data/knowledge syntheses produced by CAFF-CBMP are designed to assist policy- and decision-
making at global, national, regional and local levels. The CBMP thereby plays a key role in supporting
CAFF’s mandate to address the conservation of Arctic biodiversity, to communicate findings to the
governments and residents of the Arctic, and to promote practices that ensure the sustainability of
the Arctic’s living resources.
Implementation of the CBMP is guided by a series of multi-year strategic plans approved by the
Arctic Council – the most recent “Phase 4” is covering 2021-2027) and was approved as a "living
document" intended to be updated after completion of the new CAFF Actions for Arctic Biodiversity,
which is CAFF’s long term strategic plan scheduled for delivery and approval by the Arctic Council in
2025.
The historical development of the CBMP framework and lessons learned over two decades was
summarized in the recent paper Development of a multi-scale monitoring programme: approaches
for the Arctic and lessons learned from the Circumpolar Biodiversity Monitoring Programme 2002-
2022 (Barry et al. 2023) while the overall lessons from implementing the terrestrial CBMP
programme were summarized by Christensen et al. (2020).
CBMP is building on existing monitoring networks that guide four ecosystem-specific Steering
Groups – CBMP-marine, CBMP-coastal, CBMP-freshwater and CBMP-terrestrial (Fig.1) – each of
which have identified Focal Ecosystem Components (FECs) to monitor. When CBMP was established,
four criteria were used to prioritize FEC attributes: (1) ecological significance as identified through
the development of conceptual ecological models; (2) relevance to ecosystem services; (3) value to
5

Arctic Indigenous Peoples, and other Arctic inhabitants; and (4) essential for management and
legislation needs (Christensen et al. 2020).
Major outputs from CBMP Steering Groups include the State of the Arctic Biodiversity Reports
(SABRs) which summarize the status and trends in key elements of the Arctic environment – as
documented in peer-reviewed literature – and provides advice on how to improve Arctic biodiversity
monitoring. The State of the Arctic Terrestrial Biodiversity Report (START) (Aronsson et al. 2021) was
published in May 2021, and based on available scientific literature, including a series of peer
reviewed articles in a special issue of the scientific journal Ambio (Schmidt & Jóhannesdóttir 2020)
and a range of CAFF scientific reports as well as other relevant information (see full list of references
in START report pages 114-123).
Figure 1. CBMP organization, leads, and coordination as of July 1, 2024
While the SABRs were milestones in the CBMP process, the basis for driving CBMP forward is the
continuous work to keep overall strategic plans updated and relevant to meet new realities, and for
each the Steering Groups to follow up on the SABR recommendations and revise work plans for
future monitoring efforts. CBMP-Marine and CBMP-Freshwater have taken the process forward and
released their Freshwater 2020-2024 Work Plan (CAFF 2020a) and Marine Implementation Plan
2021-2024 (CAFF 2021b), respectively. These plans follow up on the State of The Arctic Freshwater
Report (SAFBR) (Lento et al. 2019) in 2019 and the State of The Arctic Marine Report (SAMBR) (CAFF
2017) in 2017, and the subsequent SAMBR updates on Marine Mammals (Kovacs et al. 2021) and
Seabirds (CAFF 2021c) in 2021.
However, the COVID 19 pandemic, followed by the strategic pause of Arctic Council work, has
impacted the work progress in CBMP, including within the Steering Groups and the momentum in
most activities. For the CBMP-Terrestrial, the pause implied that the scoping process of developing a
new work plan was stalled by March 2022.
6

With the gradual resumption of Arctic Council work since August 2023, the focus of the CBMP Co-
Chairs and Steering Group leads, together with the CAFF Secretariat, has been on restarting work in
the Steering Groups. In September 2024 the CAFF Board approved an extension on all existing CBMP
workplans, including the CBMP Strategic Plan, until 2027. In spring 2024 the CBMP Terrestrial co-
leads, technical team, and CAFF Chair developed a plan to advance the scoping process.
The North American Terrestrial Scoping Workshop was the second step, building on the initial ideas
from the Nordic workshop, towards creating a CBMP Terrestrial Implementation Plan. The workshop
drafted a series of “project ideas” to complement the tentative ideas from the Nordic workshop. The
insights gathered here and in the Nordic Scoping Worksop Report, will feed into the subsequent
Russian CBMP Terrestrial Workshop and, ultimately, the CBMP Terrestrial Implementation Plan.
2. Workshop Proceedings
2.1. Session 1: Workshop introduction and overview of START
Vegetation in the State of the Arctic Terrestrial Biodiversity Report
Donald McLennan
Key findings from the START Report
• Significant increase in vegetation productivity across the Arctic, especially in the low Arctic, due
to increased mean summer temperatures.
• Earlier green-up and flowering, with an increase in shrubs and grasses at the expense of lichens
and mosses.
• Non-native plant species are increasing locally in areas with human activity, though most are not
invasive.
• Insufficient data for comprehensive long-term monitoring.
Monitoring summary
• Insufficient data overall, with exceptions like the ITEX program.
• Remote sensing has been used but mostly at 250 meters resolution, which is not detailed
enough for most indicators of change
Advice for monitoring
• Investigate causality and expand in-situ time series.
• Utilize plant-based vegetation surveys and consider biotic and abiotic drivers.
• Increase monitoring efforts for all FECs and address data gaps, especially for food species.
• Use higher spatial and temporal resolution remote sensing products.
Potential next steps
7

• Increase the use of new and more high-resolution remote sensing products and terrestrial
ecosystem mapping.
• Link remote sensing and terrestrial ecosystem mapping to ground-based monitoring input on
tundra ecosystems.
• Use process-based conceptual modeling to link spatial data, EBVs, and FECs.
Discussion after the presentation
• Integration with Freshwater Monitoring:
o Joseph suggested integrating freshwater monitoring with terrestrial ecosystem mapping,
particularly around areas like Cambridge Bay, which has extensive freshwater data.
o Integration with terrestrial ecosystem mapping can identify threats to freshwater
ecosystems such as permafrost-driven mass wasting and changes in flooding regimes
• Indigenous Knowledge contribution:
o There is an opportunity to collaborate with Indigenous Peoples as land users in the
ground-truthing process for remote sensing, leveraging their extensive use of and
knowledge of the land.
• Technical and collaborative efforts:
o Discussion on the potential collaboration with the Circumpolar Architecture Science
initiative to scale up remote sensing and mapping efforts.
o Emphasis on the need for better use of new remote sensing technologies and sensors to
enhance monitoring capabilities.
• Challenges and opportunities:
o Addressing the challenge of maintaining long-term monitoring networks and the need
for more local studies linked to remote sensing for broader extrapolation.
o The importance of including higher resolution data and the potential for using Landsat
and Sentinel data for broader area mapping.
Arthropods in the State of the Arctic Terrestrial Biodiversity Report
Casey Burns
Key findings from START report
• Arthropod FECs: Six main FECs were discussed: pollinators, decomposers, prey for vertebrates,
blood feeders, predators, and parasitoids. These groups are not mutually exclusive, and a single
species can fall into multiple categories.
• Monitoring Gaps: The presentation highlighted significant gaps in arthropod monitoring across
the Arctic, with Greenland showing relatively better coverage.
• Site-Specific Data: Most data come from specific sites like Zackenberg, showing variable trends
in arthropod populations.
• Arthropod fauna is habitat-specific.
• Cryptic and genetic diversity is poorly known.
8

• Communities are highly variable in time and space.
• Summer temperature is likely less important than other variables like soil moisture and
phenology.
• Increased phenological mismatches due to climate change.
Recommendations
• Need for long-term monitoring with predictable financing.
• Improved species inventories and understanding of ecological roles.
• Enhanced communication and collaboration among experts.
• Utilization of new technologies like DNA barcoding and remote sensing.
Discussion after the presentation
• Capacity Issues: There may be a lack of experts in Canada to analyze arthropod samples,
highlighting a bottleneck in capacity.
• Technological Advances: The potential of DNA barcoding and other technologies to help with
species identification was discussed, though it was noted that these cannot completely replace
the need for taxonomists.
• Communication and Relevance: The importance of communicating the relevance of arthropod
monitoring to managers and policymakers was emphasized. This includes educating them on the
ecological roles of arthropods and their importance to biodiversity.
• Interconnections: There is a need for better integration and communication between different
monitoring groups, such as freshwater and terrestrial, to address the interconnectedness of
ecosystems.
Mammals in the State of the Arctic Terrestrial Biodiversity Report
Jim Lawler
Key findings from START report
• The focal ecosystem components (FECs) for mammals include large herbivores, small herbivores,
and medium predators; overall, there is insufficient data for medium herbivores, large
predators, and small predators.
o Caribou and reindeer: Populations are generally in decline, especially the Barren-ground
Caribou herds in North America.
o Muskoxen: Populations have increased overall, but specific herds on Banks and Victoria
Islands have declined.
o Lemmings: No clear trend in population changes, but some areas show declines where
voles are present.
9

o Arctic fox: No clear trend in population changes, with variations due to management
activities and other factors.
• Drivers of change: Climate change and associated increased weather variability is the primary
driver affecting biodiversity, abundance, and ecological function. Other factors include
pathogens and human activities.
Recommendations
• Emphasized the need for harmonized protocols, increased cooperation among expert groups,
and more research on abundance and demographics.
Discussion after the presentation
• Lemmings and voles: There was a discussion on the impact of voles on lemming populations and
the potential consequences for predators. It was noted that voles might not fully replace
lemmings as prey due to differences in size and nutritional value.
• Winter ecology: The importance of winter ecology for lemmings was highlighted, with
suggestions to include more winter data in monitoring efforts.
• Integration with Freshwater Group: The need for better integration between terrestrial and
freshwater monitoring was discussed, particularly in areas like Cambridge Bay where there is
significant data overlap.
Birds in the State of the Arctic Terrestrial Biodiversity Report
Knud Falk
Key findings from START report
• Birds in the Arctic are unique due to their migratory patterns, with only a few species remaining
in the Arctic year-round.
• Significant declines in bird populations, particularly in the East Asia flyway, while some
populations in the African-Eurasian flyway are stable or increasing.
• Geese populations are increasing in some areas, causing ecological impacts, while other species
are experiencing declines.
• High Arctic regions have limited data on bird populations, highlighting a need for more
monitoring.
Recommendations
• Safeguard and sustain long-term monitoring projects.
• Expand targeted monitoring for species with unknown or uncertain trends.
• Adopt new and emerging technologies for monitoring including Motus bird tracking.
• Increase collaboration with Indigenous Knowledge holders to improve understanding and
coverage.
• Harmonize long-term studies to make reliable assessments of status and trends.
10

Discussion after the presentation
• Integration of birds monitoring:
o Progress in AMBI (Arctic Migratory Birds Initiative) may be due to specific requests and
work plans that guide actions and funding.
o There was a discussion on the need to integrate bird monitoring across different groups
(terrestrial, freshwater, coastal) to avoid segmentation, recognize many bird’s diverse
life history traits and improve data collection.
• Challenges and opportunities:
o The importance of involving Indigenous communities and Indigenous Guardians
programs in monitoring efforts was highlighted.
o The need for regular reporting and using platforms like the Arctic Biodiversity Dashboard
to communicate findings more frequently was discussed.
• Technical and methodological improvements:
o The potential for using citizen science and new technologies to enhance bird monitoring
was mentioned.
o The importance of power analysis and understanding the limits of data for effective
monitoring was emphasized.
• Specific issues:
o The impact of overabundant geese on Arctic ecosystems was discussed, with a focus on
the need for management strategies.
o The challenges of monitoring bird populations in the high Arctic due to limited data and
harsh conditions were noted.
2.2. Session 2. Identify ways to better include Indigenous Knowledge
Inuit Circumpolar Council (ICC) Protocols for Equitable and Ethical Engagement
Sophie Crump
ICC 2022 General Assembly Declaration (item 11) directs ICC to to implement the Circumpolar Inuit
Protocols for Ethical and Equitable Engagement at the international level to force a paradigm shift
within institutions and forums that guarantees nothing about us, without us.
The Circumpolar Inuit Protocols for Ethical and Equitable Engagement (EEE Protocols) specifies eight
protocols:
11

1. ‘Nothing About Us Without Us’ – Always Engage with Inuit. This includes implementing
UNDRIP1, involving Inuit from the start of a project, and that free prior and informed consent
which includes the right to say yes, yes with conditions, or no.
2. Recognize Indigenous Knowledge in its Own Right – including that Indigenous Knowledge
must not be translated, integrated into, or validated by science. Indigenous Knowledge has its
own methodologies and objectives and makes its own unique contributions.
3. Practice Good Governance – Inuit governance structures must be respected and power
dynamics embedded in formal processes must be addressed. Focus on reciprocity and giving
back (e.g. with information in accessible formats, funding, equipment, etc.).
4. Communication with Intent – Listen more than you speak and come to the table with
humility and respect. Gather as we gather – meetings may require unstructured time, or a
preference for smaller more informal gatherings.
5. Exercising Accountability – Building Trust - Be accountable and build your capacity, take
responsibility to educate yourself.
6. Building Meaningful Partnerships – Follow processes that support multiple forms of
knowledge and holistic understanding; support Inuit driven research and monitoring
7. Information, Data Sharing, Ownership and Permissions - uphold Indigenous data
sovereignty, enable direct access to information and data generated or gathered in Inuit
homelands.
8. Equitably Fund Inuit Representation and Knowledge – evaluate, reform, and work to
address inequities in funding structures.
ICC definition of Indigenous Knowledge (IK)
• ICC defines Indigenous Knowledge (IK) as “a systematic way of thinking applied to phenomena
across biological, physical, cultural, and spiritual systems. It includes insights based on evidence
and acquired through direct and long-term experiences, extensive and multigenerational
observation, lessons, and skills. Indigenous Knowledge has developed over millennia and is still
developing in a living process, including knowledge acquired today and in the future, and it is
passed on from generation to generation.” Under this definition, Indigenous Knowledge goes
beyond observations and ecological knowledge, offering a unique way of knowing to identify
research needs and apply to research, monitoring, assessments, decision-making, policy and
overall understanding the Arctic – it is a way of life.
Discussions and questions after the presentation
• Distinguishing between local knowledge and Indigenous Knowledge: There was a discussion on
how to handle local knowledge alongside Indigenous Knowledge, emphasizing that Indigenous
Peoples are a clearly defined rights-holding group (e.g. under UNDRIP) whereas local knowledge
is a term without a clear definition. Conflation between these two terms can contribute to
1 United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP). UNDRIP affirms the Inuit right to
engage in the governance of all things related to us and our lands, territories and resources. This includes all
research, economic, and decision- and policy-making activities.
12

undermining Indigenous Peoples’ rights, and there is therefore a need to be clear about what is
being referred to by Indigenous Knowledge, and what is being referred to by local knowledge,
and ensuring that these are not conflated.
• Engagement process: It was highlighted that the process of engaging with Indigenous
communities in North America has become more robust, involving meetings with tribal
governments or hunters’ and trappers’ organizations etc., and requirements for letters of
authorization and data sovereignty agreements.
• Consultation complexity: The complexity of consultation processes in Canada was discussed,
noting the involvement of multiple organizations and the need for clear points of engagement.
The SIKU app – a digital platform for Indigenous Knowledge
Billy Nichol (virtual presentation)
• Overview: The SIKU app is a mobile and web platform developed by the Arctic Eider Society,
designed for harvesters to use out on the land without internet connections. It includes tools for
GPS, safety, and data collection.
• Features:
o Maps: Includes satellite imagery and Indigenous place names.
o Wildlife observations: Users can make observations about wildlife, which are linked to
Indigenous terminology in various dialects.
o Ice safety: Tools for reporting dangerous ice conditions using Indigenous environmental
terminology.
o Tracking: Users can track their movements and make observations about wildlife
harvests.
• Data stewardship: Users own their data and can choose to share it with projects. Projects must
still follow all ethical and permitting obligations of the region they are working in.
• Project examples
o Qikiqtait Project: Collects baseline data for a proposed protected area around the
Belcher Islands.
o Goose Watch: Tracks spring goose migration for hunters.
o Arctic Sentinels: Focuses on insect monitoring and other environmental observations.
• Principles: The app is based on principles of
o Respect for Indigenous Knowledge and rights holders
o Intellectual property ownership
o Support for self-determination in research, education and stewardship
o Integrity of information
Discussion after the presentation
• Sustainability and interoperability: Questions were raised about the sustainability of the app
and its capacity to maintain data management. Billy explained that the app is labor-intensive to
13

build but aims for stability. Interoperability with other platforms is a focus to avoid siloed
databases.
• Engagement with Greenland: There was a question about the app's engagement with
Greenland, and Billy mentioned that there are some interest from users in Greenland, so far
mainly in relation to reporting on sea ice conditions.
• Adding communities: The process of adding communities to the app is based on demand, and it
is not difficult to add new communities. The challenge is more in learning to navigate different
governance structures and adding relevant biota and new terminology.
• Indigenous environmental terminology: The app uses Indigenous environmental terminology
which helps retain in-depth knowledge embedded in Indigenous languages.
Designing a Monitoring Plan in a Co-production of Knowledge Perspective – lessons Learned
Tahzay Jones
Key points
• The Coastal Group's monitoring plan was designed to support the co-production of knowledge,
rooted in Indigenous Knowledge (IK) and a food security lens.
• Indigenous Knowledge holders were involved from the beginning, participating in workshops
and contributing as authors to the coastal plan.
• The implementation plan included identifying coastal experts, evaluating co-production efforts,
mapping “coastscapes”, and developing knowledge maps.
• Community meetings were held to confirm and gather additional information, ensuring
transparency and respect for Indigenous Knowledge.
• The plan aimed to align scientific studies with Indigenous Knowledge studies, mapping out
where these studies were relevant to the communities.
Lessons learned
• Regular check-ins are crucial to address any missteps and build trust.
• Timing and funding are significant challenges, requiring careful planning to respect community
schedules and ensure adequate compensation.
• Engaging Indigenous Knowledge holders from the start and maintaining their involvement
throughout the process is essential for successful co-production of knowledge.
Discussion after the presentation
• The importance of paying Indigenous Knowledge holders for their time and contributions was
highlighted, with a focus on compensating them for participation rather than specific
knowledge.
• The need to respect existing governance structures and work through them to identify
appropriate participants was emphasized.
14

• The challenge of engaging multiple communities and the high cost of doing so was discussed,
with a suggestion to hold regional meetings to bring together Indigenous Knowledge holders
from different areas.
2.3. Session 3. Identifying data audiences and communicating the relevance of CBMP Data
How can CBMP data be used in global reporting?
Jen Lento
A summary of needs and opportunities, existing and potential users of CBMP monitoring data
within/outside Arctic Council, including linkages to other bodies: From FEC’s to global reporting
formats.
Key points
• Relevance and visibility: Emphasized the importance of making CBMP data more visible and
relevant to national and global reporting. Highlighted the need for CBMP data to be used in
national reporting to the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) and other global frameworks.
• Harmonization of indicators: Discussed the harmonization of CBMP indicators with global
reporting structures and standards, particularly the Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs)
framework. This alignment helps translate CBMP data into formats that are useful for global
reporting.
• Engagement with national and international bodies: Stressed the importance of engaging with
national governments and international bodies to ensure CBMP data is utilized effectively. This
includes working with other Arctic Council WG and other relevant bodies and organizations.
• Use of monitoring plans: Mentioned the need to update and seek harmonization of monitoring
plans to facilitate alignment with current methodologies and technologies. This includes
incorporating new methods like eDNA and drones.
• Data management and accessibility: Highlighted the importance of making CBMP data
accessible and usable through proper data management practices. This includes options of
creating a centralized database for existing and ongoing monitoring data and following global
data, metadata and analytic pipeline standards, while also respecting and upholding Indigenous
data sovereignty.
Questions and discussions
• Principles:
o Respect for Indigenous Knowledge and rights holders
o Intellectual property ownership
o Support for self-determination in research, education and stewardship
o Integrity of information
• Relevance to national goals
o Discussion on the importance of more explicitly tying CBMP data to national goals
and mandates to ensure relevance and support from national governments.
15

o Emphasis on the need to engage with management and decision-makers to highlight
the benefits of CBMP data in saving time and resources.
• Engagement with NGOs
o Highlighted the role of non-governmental organizations (NGOs) in exerting political
pressure and advocating for the use of CBMP data.
o Mentioned the potential for NGOs to lobby for the inclusion of CBMP data in
national and international reporting frameworks.
• Strategic initiatives
o Identified the need for strategic initiatives to communicate the value of CBMP data
and prioritize FECs (Focal Ecosystem Components) for monitoring.
o Discussed the importance of making direct asks to managers for support in
implementing CBMP monitoring plans.
• Harmonization of methods
o Discussion on the need to harmonize monitoring methods across different regions
and organizations to ensure data comparability.
o Emphasized the importance of using standardized methods while allowing for some
flexibility to accommodate national protocols – and locally relevant FECs/attributes
co-developed with Indigenous Knowledge Holders.
• New monitoring technologies
o Mentioned the potential for incorporating new monitoring technologies like eDNA
and drones into CBMP monitoring plans.
o Discussed the need to keep monitoring plans updated with the latest methodologies
and technologies.
o Better use of satellites and advancing technologies
o Advancement in indicator production
Key Takeaways
• The presentation and discussions highlighted the importance of making CBMP data relevant and
visible to national and global reporting frameworks.
• Emphasized the need for harmonization of indicators and methods to ensure data comparability
and usability.
• Stressed the importance of engaging with national governments, international bodies, and NGOs
to advocate for the use of CBMP data.
• Identified the need for strategic initiatives to communicate the value of CBMP data and prioritize
monitoring efforts.
16

Connecting to international needs – Translating FECs to EBVs
Mike Gill
Key points
• Overview of EBVs: The concept of Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) and their role as
intermediaries between data collection and global biodiversity indicators were expalined. He
emphasized that EBVs are independent of measurement methods and focus solely on measuring
biodiversity change.
• Mapping FECs to EBVs to indicators: The feasibility of cross-walking Focal Ecosystem
Components (FECs) (and their consequent parameters and attributes) from the CBMP terrestrial
plan to EBVs were sumamrized. The CBMP terrestrial plan covers all six EBV classes and 20 of the
22 candidate EBVs indicating natural and broad-based alignment to the global variables. This
then allowed an assessment of the potential for CBMP Terrestrial data to populate the adopted
indicators from the Global Plan for Nature. This analysis showed adequte coverage of a number
of indicators covering Targets 1 through 8 of the global plan.
• Indicator strategy: The last CAFF-CBMP Indicator Strategy was published in 2008. Given the
importance and rapid advancement of indicator methodologies and their impact in national,
regional and global biodiversity policy, the CBMP needs a new indicator strategy to identify
alignments with existing indicators and with regional, national, sub-national and community
scale priorities.
• Workflows and “data cubes”: The concept of workflows and data cubes to structure monitoring
systems and produce scalable products was explored, highlighting the importance of creating
reproducible recipes for indicators to streamline data collection and reporting.
• Global and national relevance: The close alignment of CBMP outputs to global processes
highlights the ease at which both Arctic-specific issues and policies and global agreements can
be accommodated. A targeted indicator strategy would ensure both scales are served while also
assessing gaps in CBMP monitoring plan coverage.
Questions and discussions
• Broad support was given for the development of an indicator strategy
• Relevance to national goals: There was a discussion on the importance of linking CBMP FECs to
national and sub-national targets and policies to engage management and ensure the program's
relevance.
• Engagement with management: Participants discussed strategies to meet with management
and highlight how CBMP can save time and money, thereby assisting Senior Arctic Officials
(SAOs) in making use of CBMP outputs to support CAFF efforts.
• International goals: While recognizing the importance of international goals, the discussion
emphasized prioritizing national goals to maintain the program's relevance and support.
• Technical challenges: The group acknowledged the technical challenges in harmonizing methods
and ensuring data comparability across different regions and monitoring programs.
17

• New monitoring methods: There was a suggestion to include a component on new monitoring
methods in the toolkit, such as eDNA and drone usage, to keep the CBMP updated with
emerging technologies.
2.4. Session 4: Improving Coordination and collaboration
Arctic Biodiversity Monitoring Toolkit
Kári Fannar Lárusson & Jen Lento
Key points
• Toolkit Overview: The Arctic Biodiversity Monitoring Toolkit, currently being developed, is
designed to address recommendations and requirements from the Circumpolar Biodiversity
Monitoring Program (CBMP). It originated from the INTERACT project and provides monitoring
professionals with advice from the CBMP and offers step-by-step guidance on implementing
CBMP monitoring plans. The toolkit includes new and emerging methodologies for monitoring
and aims to harmonize Focal Ecosystem Components (FECs) across ecosystem groups. It
supports the ongoing development of monitoring guidance and contributes to the assessment of
monitoring capacity.
• Components: The toolkit includes a user manual, an FEC selection tool, a map of monitoring
locations and data sources, and a compilation of CBMP recommendations and advice.
• User Guidance: Users can select relevant focal ecosystem components (FECs) and secure
guidance on sampling methods, indicators, and harmonized methods for monitoring. The toolkit
aims to promote coordinated and harmonized monitoring approaches.
• Harmonization Efforts: The toolkit will help harmonize FECs, parameters, and attributes across
different groups (terrestrial, freshwater, marine, coastal). It will also provide updated
recommendations for sampling protocols.
Discussions after the presentation
• Relevancy and Engagement: Emphasis on engaging management by linking CBMP FECs to
national targets and policies. Highlighting the importance of demonstrating how CBMP efforts
can save time and money.
• NGO Partnerships: Recognizing the value of engaging with NGOs to influence political pressure
and support for CBMP efforts.
• Metadata and Data Sources: Importance of having an online version of metadata for monitoring
locations and published Indigenous Knowledge studies or Indigenous Knowledge-derived
information. This would be valuable for managers overseeing scientists.
• Methods and Protocols: Discussion on the complexity of adopting harmonized methods and the
potential for expert networks to recommend protocols. Mention of piloting with pollinators.
• Cross-Cutting Themes: Identifying key themes like extreme weather events, invasive species,
and food security that are important across all groups.
• Novel Techniques: Consideration of including novel techniques in the toolkit and addressing the
challenge of keeping methods up-to-date.
18

2.5. Session 5: Needs for updating monitoring protocols and identify new technologies
The discussion session was based on the Session 4 introduction on the recent development of the
Arctic Biodiversity Monitoring Toolkit and the current opportunities for directing the toolkit
development to fit the new and upcoming CBMP Implementation Plans.
• There is a need of promoting validating new technologies, such as wider use of remote sensing
and new devices for monitoring (drones, automated recordings etc.); the existing networks are
already automatically adopting new technologies, but CBMP may help guide more standardised
application.
• Participants highlighted the importance of harmonizing long-term studies, improving data
coordination, and leveraging citizen science and emerging technical tools to support monitoring.
• It is challenging to standardize protocols across research stations and monitoring networks.
• There was consensus on the need for ongoing review and adaptation of protocols to ensure they
remain relevant and effective, with a focus on collaboration and co-production of knowledge.
2.6. Session 6. Review conceptual models in the Arctic Biodiversity Monitoring Plan and FECs
Knud Falk
The session was introduced with a summary of the recent discussions at the Nordic Scoping
Workshop around the needs for revising the overall terrestrial conceptual model.
The Nordic discussions centred around the CBMP ambition of “ecosystem-based monitoring” and
how it could be promoted better by moving away from the separate taxonomic subgroups
(vegetation, arthropods, birds, mammals) as the organisational approach in the terrestrial plan. See
full summary of arguments in Nordic Scoping Report. It was suggested to restructure the Terrestrial
monitoring plan to not have the different taxonomic subgroups, but to have one CBMP terrestrial
conceptual ecosystem model, and one working group.
However, the linkages to other CBMP Groups (Freshwater, Coastal, Marine) in such as revised
conceptual model was not part of the discussion but based on other discussions – at the Nordic
workshop and here with the North American participants – that is an aspect to work on.
Key points
• Historical context: The CBMP conceptual models have evolved over time, with the latest
versions depicted in the START report (the overall model as well as the specific ones depicted for
each taxonomic group. in the). The models showed an evolution from detailed scientific
representations to more integrated ecosystem thinking. The recent “coastscapes” created by the
CBMP Coastal and co-produced with Indigenous Knowledge Holders, showed a new approach.
• Purpose of conceptual models: The session discussed the role of conceptual models in framing
the understanding of Arctic ecosystems, identifying key system elements, processes, and
relationships, and informing the selection and revision of FECs, including FECs based on
Indigenous Knowledge.
19

• Indigenous Knowledge (IK): There was a strong emphasis on better representing Indigenous
Knowledge into the conceptual models, to better reflect the interconnectedness of ecosystem
components and the perspectives of Indigenous communities.
• Simplification and prioritization: The need to simplify models and prioritize key drivers and FECs
was highlighted to make the models more practical and actionable.
• Project-based approach: It was suggested to develop models related to specific high-impact
projects or drivers, such as climate change, food security, and extreme weather events, rather
than attempting a holistic revision of all models.
• Review and revision process: A review of existing models was proposed to identify gaps and
inconsistencies, followed by targeted revisions to enhance their relevance and utility.
• The relatively radical suggestion from the Nordic Scoping Workshop on building one “whole
ecosystem conceptual model” was not fully embraced at the North American workshop – but a
working group could be established to review current models and explore new options.
Discussed action points
• Review conceptual models: Establish a working group to review existing conceptual models and
identify gaps and inconsistencies.
• Engage Indigenous Knowledge Holders: Engage in discussions with the Permanent Participants,
to identify how best to be able to engage in the CBMP across Ecosystem Groups in the CBMP –
including in the modeling process.
• Develop project-based models: Establish a working group to prioritize and develop models
related to key drivers and high-impact projects.

• Capacity considerations: Acknowledge limited capacity for producing extensive scientific

• Resource briefs: Develop two-page resource briefs for quick dissemination.
• Co-produced products: Collaborate with Permanent Participants for co-produced products and

• Relevance and engagement: Emphasis on linking CBMP efforts to national targets and policies to

for support from managers.

influence national monitoring programs.
